title: The Wild World of Sovereign Citizens
summary: Explainer on sovereign-citizen traffic-stop behaviour and a self-identified sovereign citizen's courtroom conduct at a mass-murder trial, weighing how dangerous the movement is.

assertions.quote: Oh, I'm not driving. I'm traveling. This is meant to give off the appearance of superiority
an individual is in violation if they fail to produce a license after being lawfully stopped by an officer

verdicts.note: Every US state requires a driver to carry and display a license on an officer's demand.
Ohio statute: an operator shall display the driver's license on demand of a peace officer and shall not refuse; this is one state's law, applied on appeal.

assertions.quote: In reality, this just means they're going to jail.

verdicts.note: A speeding and plate stop escalated into removal from the car, arrest and four charges including obstruction after the driver said 'no contract' and refused ID; this is one case, not a rate.
Review says traffic stops with sovereigns become long, combative standoffs where officers often must break windows and remove them physically; it does not quantify arrests, towing or extra charges.

assertions.quote: The FBI took that classification a step further and has actually deemed them domestic terrorists.

verdicts.note: The review cites a 2010 FBI document that calls sovereign citizens anti-government extremists and the movement a domestic terrorist threat.
The FBI's own Law Enforcement Bulletin states the FBI considers sovereign-citizen extremists a domestic terrorist movement (the label attaches to the extremists, not every believer).
Review states sovereign citizens have been labeled by the FBI as a terrorist threat and quotes the FBI's extremist definition.

assertions.quote: There are scripts that exist that tell sovereign citizens how they should behave when pulled over

verdicts.note: Researchers and police training material document widely shared scripts, phrases and document templates.
The driver pulled out a binder of prepared texts and repeated 'no contract' and 'does not give consent'; in court he recited sui juris, UCC 1-308 and flesh-and-blood formulas. This is one case.
OPCA document and courtroom 'formal trappings' are stereotyped and nearly unchanged since 2012, but the passage is about court filings, not police encounters.
Affiliates' language and use of legal terms are formulaic and materials are recycled, but the source is not specific to police encounters.
Adherents share a belief that reciting set phrases ('I am a living being', 'I do not consent') gives immunity, including from licence demands.
Review lists recurring stop tactics: demanding officers prove jurisdiction, refusing to answer, saying 'I do not consent', and cracking the window claiming it is broken.

assertions.quote: They charged customers between $450 and $2,000 for a diplomatic identification card that bestowed sovereign status.
Supposedly to enjoy diplomatic immunity from paying taxes and from stops and arrest by law enforcement.

verdicts.note: FBI reports sellers of 'sovereign status' diplomatic ID cards that promised immunity from stops and arrests were convicted; the cards gave no such protection.
